new_statements.rule_in_words: Default word stress falls on the penultimate syllable; words whose stress is elsewhere (in practice mostly final) are individually marked in Turner & Turner's 1971 dictionary, i.e. penultimate is the regular position with lexically/morphologically specified exceptions. (van der Hulst, Rice & Wetzels 2010: 282, summarising Turner 1966/1967, add: one primary stress per word, stressed syllable lengthened; stress may be displaced to the final syllable by the word's position in the sentence; plural can be marked by stress shift, lenala sg. penult-stressed vs. pl. final-stressed.)
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described. van der Hulst et al. 2010 (after Turner) say there is a single primary stress per word; Turner 1982 marks only 'primary word stress'.
new_statements.exceptions: Oltrogge: non-penultimate stresses are 'otherwise marked' in the source dictionary; inflected verb citation forms carry stress on the stem-final syllable (= word-penultimate before the monosyllabic suffix). van der Hulst et al. 2010 < Turner 1966/1967: displacement to the final syllable conditioned by sentence position; morphological stress shift marking plural (lenala); grammatical-phonological interactions. Turner 1967: 31 (snippet) describes clause-final words stressed on either the penultimate or the final syllable with different intonation contours.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level default (dictionary citation forms). Turner 1967 p. 31 treats stress placement in the clause-final word together with clause intonation, and Turner's 1982 stress-marked text shows the same word with penultimate or final stress in different sentence positions (l-acol 'the turtle'), so surface stress is partly phrase-conditioned; in that text a crude count of accent marks gives roughly 60% penultimate, 20% final, 12% earlier (my own heuristic tally, not from any source).
new_statements.identity_note: All sources refer to the Highland (Sierra) variety = Glottolog high1242. Oltrogge 1977 calls the language 'Tequistlateco' but states explicitly (p. 25) that his data 'represent the highland dialect as recorded in Turner and Turner (1971)' (Turner's fieldwork base: San Matias Petacaltepec). The 1970 ILV Diccionario de la Sierra Chontal is from Santa Maria Ecatepec (also Highland). Not to be confused with Lowland/Huamelultec Chontal (lowl1260), for which Waterhouse & Morrison 1950 report phonemic stress, nor with extinct Tequistlatec proper of Tequisistlan.

sources.note: p. 211: 'primary word stress is indicated by an acute accent' - every word in the text is stress-marked (speaker from San Matias Petacaltepec) but no placement rule is stated. Marks are predominantly penultimate but final and antepenultimate stresses occur, incl. doublets (l-acol 'the turtle' with final stress in sentence 1, initial in sentence 5; a-mafka ~ a-mafka with final stress).
